title: Customers pay with 5, 10, or 20 unit notes for a 5 unit item and you start with no change. Determine whether you can give correct change to every customer in order. Explain the greedy strategy, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Lemonade Change (Greedy Change-Making at a Counter)

s1_definition.profdef: Lemonade Change decides whether a cashier starting with no float can give correct change to a queue of customers paying with fixed note values. The greedy rule keeps running counts of each note and, when change is owed, dispenses the largest notes first, preserving small notes which are scarce and more flexible. It fails the instant a required change cannot be formed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India branch counter accepts fixed-value notes for a fixed-price service and must return exact change from the notes it has collected so far. It hands out larger notes first to keep its flexible small notes in reserve.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give change using the largest notes first to hoard the scarce small notes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Lemonade Change decides whether a cashier starting with no float can give correct change to a queue of customers paying with fixed note values. The greedy rule keeps running counts of each note and, when change is owed, dispenses the largest notes first, preserving small notes which are scarce and more flexible. It fails the instant a required change cannot be formed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India branch counter accepts fixed-value notes for a fixed-price service and must return exact change from the notes it has collected so far. It hands out larger notes first to keep its flexible small notes in reserve.

**One line to remember:** Give change using the largest notes first to hoard the scarce small notes.

sections.s2_technical:
We track how many five-unit and ten-unit notes we currently hold; twenty-unit notes are never used for change so we need not count them. A five-unit payment needs no change, so we simply keep the note. A ten-unit payment needs five in change, so we must have a five. A twenty-unit payment needs fifteen in change, and we prefer one ten and one five over three fives, because fives are more useful for future ten-unit payments. If at any point the required change cannot be assembled, we fail immediately.

The core logic is `if (pay == 5) fives++; else if (pay == 10) { if (fives == 0) return false; fives--; tens++; } else { if (tens > 0 && fives > 0) { tens--; fives--; } else if (fives >= 3) fives -= 3; else return false; }`. A concrete check: payments 5, 5, 5, 10, 20 succeed, while 5, 5, 10, 10, 20 fail because the last twenty cannot be changed. Senior nuance: the greedy preference for giving larger notes first is provably optimal here because fives dominate in flexibility, and the whole scan is linear time and constant space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a branch counter for a fixed-fee service where customers pay with five, ten, or twenty unit notes and the counter starts with no float. The counter must return exact change to each customer in the order they arrive, using only notes collected from earlier customers. The team wants to know whether a given arrival sequence can be served fully. This is exactly how Lemonade Change works: greedily give larger notes first and fail if change cannot be made.

The code defines a `CounterChangeService` with `canServeAll(payments)` using the greedy counts. A `Demo` provides a payment sequence and logs whether all customers can be served.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is payments five, five, five, ten, twenty. Step 1: the first three fives need no change, so the counter now holds three fives. Step 2: the ten needs five in change; a five is available, so the counter gives it and now holds two fives and one ten. Step 3: the twenty needs fifteen in change; the counter prefers one ten plus one five, both available, so it gives them and now holds one five and zero tens. Step 4: every customer has been served with exact change, so we return true. Had the sequence instead ended needing fifteen with only fives and no ten, the greedy would give three fives, and if fewer than three fives were present it would fail.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:50:15 PM com.bank.counter.service.CounterChangeService canServeAll
INFO: All customers served with correct change
Oct 27, 2026 9:50:15 PM com.bank.counter.CounterChangeApplication main
INFO: Can serve all customers = true
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Lemonade Change is a greedy problem where the key realisation is that not all notes are equally useful. I track running counts of the five-unit and ten-unit notes I hold, and I ignore the twenty-unit notes for change because they are never handed back. A five-unit payment needs no change, a ten-unit payment needs a single five, and a twenty-unit payment needs fifteen, which I can make either as a ten plus a five or as three fives.

The greedy decision that makes this correct is to always prefer giving a ten plus a five over three fives when I owe fifteen. Fives are the scarce, flexible currency because every ten-unit payment consumes one, so I hoard them by spending larger notes first. This is provably optimal here, and the algorithm simply fails the moment a required amount of change cannot be assembled from what I currently hold. The whole thing is a single linear pass using only a couple of counters.

At the National Bank of India I used this exact logic at a branch counter for a fixed-fee service where the till started empty and had to return exact change to customers in arrival order using only notes collected from earlier customers. I ran the greedy check to confirm whether a given arrival sequence could be fully served and to alert staff before a change shortage occurred. Explaining why fives are the scarce resource, the prefer-larger-notes-first rule, and the immediate-failure condition is what shows an interviewer I understand why this greedy strategy is both correct and efficient.
